lines: A plant's own chart starts crying wolf, and eventually the people watching it just stop listening.
Split the exact same readings by which machine actually made each one, and the mystery dissolves into two perfectly steady machines running side by side.
The chart was never unstable. The table underneath it was just missing a column.
Two very different questions get asked of the same number, and it helps to keep them apart.
One question is about the process itself: is it behaving the way it always has?
The other is about the customer: will this particular part actually do its job?
A process can answer the first question beautifully and the second one badly, in either direction.
Run the actual numbers rather than taking that on faith.
One coating reading sits right inside the band this process has always produced, nothing unusual about it at all.
That same reading sits above the ceiling the customer actually needs.
Stable process. Bad part. Both true at once, and neither fact cancels the other.
Here's something worth reasoning out before the chart answers it for you.
A handful of extra pattern rules get added on top of the basic three-sigma check, built to catch drifts that check alone would miss.
Is there any cost to adding them, or is it pure upside?
answer: There's a cost, and it follows from what sensitivity even means.
Any rule sharp enough to notice a real drift sooner is, by that same sharpness, going to notice an ordinary run of noise sooner too.

lines: So how big is that cost, measured rather than guessed at?
Running the lone basic check alone, a false alarm shows up roughly every three hundred seventy points, which lines up almost exactly with the published reference figure.
Add in the extra pattern rules, and that gap collapses down to roughly every ninety points, again matching the same published source closely.
That matched number turns out to hide something worth saying out loud.
It belongs to exactly three of the extra rules, not the whole family of them.
Bring in one more, the one that watches for a long run of points sitting on a single side, and the gap between false alarms shrinks again, on top of what the first three already cost.
A borrowed headline figure stops meaning what you think it means the moment the rule set under it changes.
Two synthetic production lines, built with the identical amount of natural spread, make a nice test case.
One sits right in the middle of what the customer will accept. The other sits shifted toward the ceiling.
Their spread-only scores land close together, as you'd expect from two processes with equal spread.
But the shifted line's second score, the one that also accounts for where it's centred, trails noticeably behind its own first score.
Pour two machines' readings into a single chart with no record of which machine made which point, and that chart trips several of the pattern rules.
Split that identical data back apart by machine, and each one, taken on its own, barely trips anything at all.
Not one physical part changed between those two views. Only the grouping did.
Follow that bad reading all the way through the paperwork it actually generates.
It creates a record of what failed, tied back to the exact inspection that found it.
A separate corrective-action record then ties back to that failure record, carrying who owns the fix and by when, and it starts life unverified.
None of this chain is even possible to build unless the original reading carried its recipe, its machine and its shift along with it.
Two kinds of limit, asking two different questions about one number.
A measured price for the extra pattern rules that lines up with the published figure.
A further, separate price for one more rule on top of that.
A centring problem that a spread-only score can hide completely.
And one chart that turns into two calm ones the moment it's split by machine.
A supervisor gets tired of the extra pattern rules firing and switches them off, keeping only the original basic check.
Does that make the basic check itself any less reliable than it was a moment earlier?
answer: It doesn't, and that's the part worth sitting with.
Each rule's own reliability is a property of that rule, full stop.
Switching the others off only removes their signals. It can't reach back and change anything about the one rule left running.
